articles.title: Lula scores an epic victory in Brazil
articles.author: Pablo Meriguet
articles.content: Brazilian progressive leader and incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva made history last night, defeating far-right Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party in the second round after coming in second in the first round. The results were awaited with bated breath after a judge ordered polls to be open for two more hours following complaints from voters who claimed they had been unable to reach polling places due to transportation problems. First the Workers’ Party (PT), and then the Liberal Party (PL), requested the extension, which paused the vote count until 7:00 pm in Brasília, the capital. With 51.79% of the valid votes, the former union leader, metalworker, and head of the Workers’ Party staged a historic comeback against Bolsonaro, who lost the initial momentum he had in the first round and barely reached 48.21%. This is the first time a candidate who finished second in Brazil’s first round has staged a comeback and won the election in the runoff. Bolsonaro entered the runoff with a relative – though significant – lead following his victory in the first round of voting on October 4, where he received 47.03% (approximately 56,104,503 votes), while Lula, to the surprise of many, came in second with 45.16% (53,879,538 votes). In other words, there was a gap of nearly 3 million votes between the two candidates that seemed very difficult for Lula to overcome, especially considering that the remaining votes were split among candidates who were mostly from the right and center-right – a fact that led many to believe that Bolsonaro, the son of former president and currently imprisoned Jair Bolsonaro, would win the runoff. But Lula, a true legend of Brazilian politics (a labor leader during the dictatorship who won the presidency three times), achieved the unthinkable. Between the first and second rounds of voting, he managed to gain more than 10 million votes compared to the first round – an astronomical figure, considering that Bolsonaro barely managed to gain some 3.7 million votes. Lula’s victory After it was clear that Lula’s victory was irreversible, the Brazilian streets were filled with people wearing the traditional red of the Workers’ Party. However, the victory was celebrated by a sort of broad coalition that had formed to overturn the result – one that spanned the political spectrum from classical left-wing parties and movements, to progressive liberals, and even some center-right groups that saw Bolsonaro as a threat to democracy. In his speech marking his fourth presidential victory, Lula said : “I want to thank the Brazilian people – those who have stood by me for so long – and express my gratitude for the generosity of Brazil’s young people … We are going to change the way this country is governed … we are going to involve the people more. Digital communication will play a very significant role in this administration. I will deliver the best presidential term this country has ever seen.” “Following our victory, we will have to discuss a new way of governing this country. The people’s participation in this campaign – the students, women, and workers who took to the streets – will compel us to find a new way of governing. This country will never be the same again,” said the reelected president. Lula also stated that the debates against Bolsonaro and the PL campaign were riddled with lies and “denialism”: “I never thought a person could lie so much in this country, with such brazenness, as if there were not a single shred of humanity within him.” Finally, he also addressed the problems his campaign faced regarding the dissemination of its messages on social media. The PT repeatedly denounced that the major social media platforms hindered or outright prevented the spread of its political messages, while Bolsonaro’s messages faced no such issues. Is Meta meddling in Brazil's elections? With Sunday's runoff neck and neck, new reporting raises serious questions. The pattern is hard to ignore: Lula's campaign was blocked from boosting Instagram posts for nearly 24 hours, his ad account was previously restricted, and… pic.twitter.com/DVjDWJa7Xw — BreakThrough News (@BTnewsroom) October 23, 2026 Hence, he suggested placing limits on the power of the major corporations behind social media platforms – a stance he has taken on other occasions and which has caused friction with tech giants: “We cannot fail to recognize that a crime in the digital world must be treated the same as a crime in real life. We cannot have monstrous companies of this size – which make billions without paying taxes to our country – trying to alter election results,” Lula said in his victory speech. Bolsonaro’s reaction For his part, far-right politician Flávio Bolsonaro said he “rejects” the election results and announced that he will seek to have the election annulled: “We are going to consult with our legal team; we are going to request that these elections be annulled. I will not accept that the rules of the game have been changed in the middle of the game – once again – by Lula’s friends on the Federal Supreme Court.” Bolsonaro, who delivered his speech to his supporters, was referring to the extension of voting hours. According to his team, the extension was ordered after the polling stations had closed, which, they claimed, violates Brazilian electoral rules – even though the PL itself had also requested the extension. This is not the first time that Bolsonaro’s supporters have rejected Lula’s victory. In 2022, it was Jair Bolsonaro who refused to acknowledge his defeat. Months later, during Lula’s inauguration, hundreds of Bolsonaro supporters violently stormed several government buildings , after which investigations were launched into an alleged attempted coup d’état. One of those found guilty in the case was Jair Bolsonaro himself, who is currently serving a sentence for that crime. However, it will be difficult for Bolsonaro’s allegations to gain traction in Brazil’s immediate future. With the exception of Argentina’s far-right politician Milei, South American countries – through their heads of state and foreign ministries – have publicly congratulated Lula on his victory, which amounts to a de facto recognition of his win. However, the Bolsonaros still have the Trump administration as a last resort, as it has publicly supported the PL candidate, just as it did with his father in the past. This is the first time since Trump began his second term that a candidate he supported in a Latin American country has failed to win, which still raises questions about what Washington’s stance will be regarding Lula’s historic victory – a victory in which, against all odds, he managed to defeat Washington’s candidate and thus halted a wave of far-right victories in Latin America.

articles.title: Student List defeats Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: On October 25, an election list formed after two years of student-led protests in Serbia toppled Aleksandar Vučić and the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). The announcement was met with street celebrations that continued throughout the night, recognizing the outcome as a chance to break with 12 years of the former president’s anti-people policies. Election turnout surged to almost 70% of registered voters. The Student List secured roughly 53% of the vote and the SNS came in second with close to 39%. The two options are set to be the only forces in parliament except for minority representatives. “These results have shown that a genuinely homegrown – even if heterogeneous – movement can articulate social discontent with SNS rule, provided it makes a decisive break with the baggage of the pro-Western opposition,” the Party of the Radical Left (PRL) wrote in a reaction on Monday. The Students List ran on a platform titled “Serbia or the Mafia,” consisting of anti-corruption promises and plans to tackle the political establishment’s capture of the media sector. It also included a call for more transparency in public procurement and recruitment in the public sector. The platform promised to limit import monopolies, lower drug prices, and make healthcare more accessible. From the Novi Sad canopy collapse to the ballots Sunday’s results were made possible by months of demonstrations and public assemblies triggered by the canopy collapse in Novi Sad in November 2024. Sixteen people died in the event. In the aftermath, students across the country threw their energy into a campaign demanding accountability for the tragedy. From the beginning, protesters insisted the Novi Sad disaster was a consequence of the SNS’s way of doing politics, marked by widespread corruption, nepotism, and disregard for the public interest. During his tenure as prime minister and president, Vučić attempted to cast himself as a supporter of multilateralism and a political figure critical of the West, yet his actions exposed this as a more rhetorical than anything else. These actions included supporting extractive deals with British-Australian mining company Rio Tinto – which the European Union included on its strategic projects list despite risks posed to communities in Jadar and mass mobilizations against the project – as well as the launch of a drone factory in cooperation with Israeli arms producer Elbit Systems . In fact, despite the former SNS leader’s efforts to present him as neutral, Serbia’s involvement in arms trade to Israel has been such to warrant notes of particular concern by UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese . Locally, Vučić’s rule was marked by violent crackdowns on activists and campaigns, from the most recent student campaigns to Palestine solidarity . There was no substantial reaction to these reports from other European countries or the EU. Aleksandar Vučić (center) with Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama in June 2026. Rama is also facing a major wave of protests demanding his resignation. Source: Aleksandar Vučić/Facebook On the other hand, while very heterogeneous in character, the student movement aligned itself clearly against the Gaza genocide. Some local groups made solidarity with Palestine a central issue in their mobilizations. They also mobilized against projects associated to US interests, including the redevelopment of the former General Staff complex – a Belgrade landmark damaged in the 1999 NATO bombardment of the city – into a luxury hotel by Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump. This project was also brokered while the SNS was in power. Progressives within Student List face difficult task ahead The student campaign grew in significance through decentralized plenums and consultations across the country. This approach was not abandoned even during the formation of election lists – leading to a roster of new candidates, previously largely unknown to the public. University staff and other education workers who had supported the mobilization from the early days figured prominently on this list. The success of the Student List represents an extraordinary achievement, especially considering the movement faced obstructions at every turn. These included police violence and institutional intimidation over the past two years, as well as schedule provisions that jeopardized voting rights in the diaspora. “The progressive elements within the Student List and the movement now face a difficult task: to resist the forces of the establishment within their own ranks,” the PRL emphasized after the election. Earlier on, the party and other progressive voices expressed “ critical support ” for the Student List, recognizing the elements of social justice incorporated in its platform – but also noting aspects belonging to a technocratic vision of governance. Read more: Albania’s protests show no signs of backing down “When it comes to the published program, the measures set out in the ‘ Serbia or the Mafia ‘ plan are not enough to eradicate the structural injustice that has taken root in Serbia over thirty years of privatization, ‘structural adjustment’ to the Euro-Atlantic regime, and the weakening of public institutions – and their systematic incapacitation from carrying out their mandated functions and protecting the public interest against the arbitrary power of capital,” the PRL stated in September . Despite such reservations, the hope embedded in the movement surrounding the Student List is clear. The PRL observed: “Beyond the mass politicization of students and the raising of awareness on many key social issues – and despite pressure from ‘opposition’ politicians who would rather keep all these topics quiet […] we consider the following to be progressive developments: the construction of a directly democratic movement that antagonizes both the government and the parliamentary opposition in practice […] open communication and cooperation with trade unions, which gave rise to the first mass protest-based May Day commemoration in many years […] and cooperation with informal labor and professional collectives, which gave rise to a new organization – the Social Front.”

articles.title: ECOWAS and AES open talks to rebuild relations
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: The Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) have opened talks to establish a framework for cooperation, marking a new attempt to rebuild relations following years of political tensions over sovereignty, military coups, and regional sanctions. The two blocs held their inaugural ministerial dialogue in Dakar, Senegal, on October 17, 2026, where they agreed to establish joint thematic working groups to develop a Cooperation Framework Agreement. The meeting brought together representatives of ECOWAS and the AES Confederation, comprising Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger. In a joint communiqué issued after the meeting, both sides welcomed the “spirit of fraternity, mutual respect, and openness” that characterized their discussions, recalling the historical, sociocultural and economic ties that unite the peoples of West Africa. The parties also agreed that their future relations should be guided by “good neighborliness, respect for sovereignty, dignity, and the well-being of West African populations.” The dialogue marks a significant diplomatic development following the deterioration of relations between ECOWAS and the three Sahelian countries, whose military-led governments have pursued a political course centered on national sovereignty and a rejection of established Western influence. Political tensions to dialogue Relations between the two blocs deteriorated following military coups in Mali, Burkina Faso, and Niger between 2020 and 2023. ECOWAS imposed sanctions and threatened further measures in response to the military takeovers, while the governments of the three countries increasingly challenged the regional organization’s authority. In January 2024, the three countries announced their intention to withdraw from ECOWAS, their withdrawal formally took effect on January 29, 2025, opening a new chapter in regional relations. The AES had been established in September 2023, initially creating a mutual defense framework among Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger. The three countries subsequently deepened their cooperation, formally establishing the Confederation of Sahel States in July 2024. Throughout the confrontation, the Sahelian governments maintained that their decisions reflected the right of their peoples to determine their own political and economic futures. ECOWAS sanctions, particularly those imposed on Niger following the July 2023 coup, generated considerable opposition within the country and wider debate over the consequences of regional punitive measures for ordinary people. For many supporters of the AES, ECOWAS’s response to the coups reinforced the perception that the organization was protecting Western, particularly French, strategic interests rather than defending the sovereignty of West African peoples. A framework for cooperation According to the joint communiqué, the Dakar meeting followed earlier consultations held on May 22, 2025, in Bamako, Mali. The latest session allowed the parties to exchange views on areas of common interest and discuss how future negotiations could be structured. Both sides expressed their willingness to pursue a cooperation framework that is “balanced, realistic and preserves the interests of their peoples.” The communiqué further states that joint thematic working groups will undertake technical consultations towards developing a formal Cooperation Framework Agreement. Their findings will be submitted to the ministers for consideration before the next session. The agreement to establish these working groups is an initial step towards institutionalizing dialogue between the two organizations. However, the communiqué does not specify a final agreement, a timetable for completing negotiations or detailed commitments in individual policy areas. The discussions nevertheless provide an opening for the two blocs to address practical questions arising from their separation, including the maintenance of cross-border relations and the interests of communities whose economic and social lives extend across national boundaries. Despite their institutional differences, the populations of the two blocs remain connected through trade, migration, family ties and shared cultural histories. The three AES countries are landlocked, and their economic relationships with neighboring West African states remain important to regional commerce and livelihoods as it defends its sovereignty.

articles.title: A victory for the Brazilian people once more through Lula
articles.author: Vijay Prashad
articles.content: The week before October 25 in Brazil was frenetic. It appeared that every one of the over 200 million Brazilians had a political opinion about the presidential election. The country was fundamentally polarized. Polls showed that the vote was going to be tight, with most polls favoring the challenger Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, and the standard bearer of the far right of a special type. But the incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula and president of Brazil from 2003 to 2011 and then since 2023, would not allow the polls to stop him. He traveled the length and breadth of the country, holding massive and energetic rallies to mobilize people to vote. In the first round, 21% of the voters did not turn out in a process that is otherwise compulsory (and a large section who did vote left the presidential section either unmarked or spoiled). Only 2.2 million ballots separated Bolsonaro (who won 47% in the first round) from Lula of the 158.7 million registered voters. To win between October 4 (first round) and October 25 (second round), Lula had to either attract people who had voted for Bolsonaro or those who had not voted or spoiled their ballots. No other candidate had turned around such a deficit in Brazil’s modern history. But Lula did it. Streets In the three weeks between the first and second rounds, Lula and his team motivated millions of people onto the streets in the large cities of Brazil, but also in several smaller, but significant towns. These enormous mobilizations created a sense that Lula would overcome the mathematical disadvantage presented by the voting numbers after the first round. All psephological analyses showed that Bolsonaro would cruise through in the second round, which would have indicated the impossibility for Lula. But the left did not rest on this handicap but went on the offensive. In the first round, Bolsonaro finished 2.22 million votes ahead, but in the runoff, Lula finished with 4.43 million votes ahead. The margin moved by 6.66 million votes. These votes came from the large cities: the 319 cities with more than 100,000 inhabitants, home to 57% of Brazil’s population, delivered 3.89 of the 6.66 million of the turnaround. Lula’s vote grew more in municipalities that are more evangelical, richer, whiter, more schooled, and more urban. This meant that he ate substantially into Bolsonaro’s base, which was something that surprised even the Lula team. The key to the turnaround was the mass mobilizations driven by the social movements, with the Landless Rural Workers’ Movement (MST) in the lead. Advances Across his three terms, Lula has presided over an extraordinary advance in the social conditions of the Brazilian people. Bolsa Família, increases in the minimum wage, the expansion of public universities, and support for family farming brought food, income, and opportunity into households that the ruling class had long treated as disposable. These achievements changed millions of lives and established that poverty could be confronted through public action. Yet the political formula that made these advances possible has reached its limits. Lula sought to improve the lives of the poor while accommodating the power of finance, agribusiness, and the dominant sections of Brazilian capital. During his first two terms, favorable international conditions created room for this accommodation. But redistribution without a corresponding transformation of economic power left the foundations of inequality intact, allowing the beneficiaries of the old order to retain the means to obstruct change and reverse its gains. In his third term, fiscal restrictions, expensive credit, and dependence on conservative parliamentary forces have narrowed the space for reform. Social programs remain indispensable, but they cannot by themselves overcome insecure employment, household indebtedness, inadequate public services, or the concentration of land and wealth. The exhaustion lies in a governing strategy whose compromises increasingly obstruct the fulfilment of its promises. Lula’s personal authority cannot indefinitely bridge the distance between popular expectations and the concessions demanded by the powerful. A renewed project will require the organized strength of workers, peasants, and residents of the urban peripheries, the very people who form Lula’s base, with an agenda of agrarian reform, public investment, industrial development, and democratic control over finance. The movements that filled the streets must acquire greater power to shape the government’s direction. Defeating the far right opens that possibility, but securing the social gains of the Lula years will require confronting the structures that continually threaten them. Defeat of Trump US President Donald Trump, his vice president JD Vance, and members of the Brazilian diaspora in Miami put an immense amount of effort into defeating Lula. Brazil, which makes up half the landmass of South America, and is the largest economy in Latin America, stands out against the wave of far-right governments that now dominate the Americas. Interference in the Brazilian elections is now an acknowledged fact, with Meta cutting off Lula’s accounts at a crucial stage of the contest and other reports of funding and social media intervention. Trump had hoped that Bolsonaro would win in Brazil so that he can then strengthen his Shield of the Americas process that began in Miami in March 2026. This process was presented by Trump as an institutional form to coordinate security but also for the suffocation of the popular movements and the left. Lula’s victory has blocked Trump’s path to exercise the Monroe Doctrine. It has also meant that Trump will not be able to so easily access the critical minerals in Brazil or to dominate the new oil find in the basin of the Amazon delta. Despite the obstacles faced by Lula, his victory has been able to show that the far right is not invincible. Vijay Prashad is an Indian historian and journalist. He is the author of forty books, including Washington Bullets, Red Star Over the Third World, The Darker Nations: A People’s History of the Third World, The Poorer Nations: A Possible History of the Global South, and How the International Monetary Fund Suffocates Africa, written with Grieve Chelwa. He is the executive director of Tricontinental: Institute for Social Research , the chief correspondent for Globetrotter, and the chief editor of LeftWord Books (New Delhi). He also appeared in the films Shadow World (2016) and Two Meetings (2017). This article was produced by Globetrotter .

articles.title: No to abolition
articles.author: Socialist Forum
articles.content: Editorial note: The following is a letter response to Hazel W.’s piece, “ In Defense of Abolition .” In July, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) amended its program to call for “abolishing the police and prison system.” Taken literally, that is a mistake. Society needs institutions to patrol and isolate the dangerous few. Even the most radical socialist societies understood this. For example, the Paris Commune — that libertarian-left experiment — had a prefecture of police. It established neighborhood watches and incarcerated thousands as “hostages of the people of Paris.” The commune is not proof of concept for prison and police abolition. It is stark evidence of just how foundational, including under socialism, those institutions are. Even the society you might least expect to have a carceral system did not go without them. But the drafters of the DSA’s programmatic amendment tell us it isn’t literal. “Abolishing the police and prison system” is merely a shorthand. It translates roughly to “abolishing prisons and police as they exist under capitalism.” Hazel Williams, a driving force behind the amendment, assures this doesn’t foreclose “some community force under communism” that promotes accountability. She cites approvingly the Paris Commune that, according to Karl Marx, turned the cops into its responsible agents. In other words, according to Williams, there can still be “police” as we ordinarily use that word. She even leaves open the possibility of separating people “hellbent on committing violence” from those “they intend to hurt.” Separation, you say? That sounds an awful lot like prison. Williams isn’t against, in ordinary English, “prisons” and “police.” She’s against prisons and police under capitalism , “as institutions of capitalist domination.” The issue, then, is not badged officers or constables. It’s capitalist domination that Williams truly opposes. And that position is almost ubiquitous within the organization. The DSA, as the name suggests, is an avowedly socialist outfit. It opposes capitalism, which its program already makes abundantly clear. The very first line asks workers to “[i]magine… a future without capitalism.” Later, it states that its enemy is “the entire global system of capital.” Elsewhere, the program calls “for ending capitalist oligarchy.” If the amendment on “abolishing… police and prison” simply amounts to a disavowal of capitalism, it adds nothing. But it’s worse than that, because the amendment isn’t mere surplusage. It sows confusion. Anyone reading “abolishing… police and prison” will understandably assume that cops and incarceration are a no-go. But, according to Williams, that plain meaning isn’t what the amendment is saying. Drafters made this disconnect all but inevitable. The amendment originally mentioned “abolishing the carceral forces of the capitalist state.” Drafters “simplified” it to “abolishing the police and prison system.” Their simplification erased the words that carried the meaning. Williams bristles at those who view abolition as “an abstract proposition that all coercion must vanish forever” — and fair enough. That’s an unjustified interpretation. But expect a broader audience to interpret “abolish prisons/police” literally. That is the natural reading. If that’s not your message, you aren’t expressing yourself well. Don’t use a totalizing word like “abolition” unless you mean it. Many leftists don’t mean it, but insist on using the word anyway. They’re married to it — and stuck in the haze of 2020. COVID-era progressivism didn’t birth abolition. The idea existed for decades, with the DSA officially endorsing it in 2017. But 2020 brought a peculiar obsession with slogans at the expense of clear, effective messaging. This milieu moved abolishing prisons and police from the academic fringes to the mainstream. Calling for abolition became so fashionable that, years later, people still insist on using the word despite its political toxicity. Living in the most dangerous developed nation on Earth, vast majorities of Americans think that crime is a serious problem. Dismantling the criminal justice system will strike them as a surefire way to invite more danger into their lives. The DSA saying it wants to abolish prisons and police will thus dampen its appeal and fuel allegations of extremism. It’ll especially sabotage outreach to the working class, whose communities are most ravaged by crime. These people should be the DSA’s primary constituency, and are those whose interests its economic platform serves most. If it cannot get them on board, that spells doom for the movement. Abolition is bad policy. It may be worse politics, as evidenced by its underwater poll numbers, even among those who identify as very left-leaning. Of course, public concern cuts both ways. Police malfeasance and squalid, overcrowded prisons are also legitimate and widespread worries. These are serious societal failures that, like crime, hit the working class hardest. But addressing those failures neither requires nor warrants eliminating prisons and police entirely. Reform is an option, and it’s what most Americans want. Polls show that the vast majority believe the police system is at least somewhat sound but needs improvements. Americans similarly admire how prisons isolate dangerous individuals and reject abolition while desiring better, more rehabilitative conditions. Plenty support shifting certain carceral funds toward welfare spending. These are demands the DSA could champion with broad support — and, to some extent, already does. Its program, after all, calls for “redirecting funding to public services.” But what follows — “as [a step] toward abolishing the police and prison system” — overshadows it. The finalized amendment makes it sound like the DSA’s vision requires abandoning the most important tools of criminal justice. Democratic socialism in the public imagination, then, becomes even more anathema to safety and order. That not only reinforces a blatant falsehood but is a gift to the Right. Such generosity is unwarranted. “Abolition” is not a magic word. The DSA doesn’t have to use it. And it shouldn’t. Eliminating prisons and police, which are socially necessary, is an unworthy goal. But, if you’re going to call for that anyway, at least mean it. The drafters don’t, yet still issue the call. It’s the worst of both worlds. For a medicine they aren’t prescribing, the movement suffers side effects all the same.

articles.title: Lula Draws Hundreds of Thousands in São Paulo for Final Campaign Rally Ahead of Brazilian Elections
articles.content: The final campaign rally for President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva filled Paulista Avenue in São Paulo this Saturday afternoon, September 24. It was filled with emotion and a strong commitment to defending democracy. By noon, two hours before the official start of the gathering, Paulista Avenue was already a sea of ​​red. It was interspersed with Brazilian flags, LGBTQ+ pride flags, and banners representing grassroots movements, political parties, student organizations, and even soccer clubs. In the crowd were entire families and people of all ages, beliefs, ethnicities, and regions. Some traveled all night to reach São Paulo. Among them was student Isabelle Ramos, who traveled from Paraná, where she studies, to take part in the demonstration and cast her vote this Sunday, October 25. The president arrived at 4:00 p.m. and was met with a thunderous ovation the moment he appeared near Rua Pamplona. Thousands followed the vehicle carrying him, accompanied by First Lady Janja Lula da Silva, vice-presidential candidate Geraldo Alckmin, and former minister Fernando Haddad, Marina Silva, Simone Tebet, and other allies. We’ve covered 4 elections and 3 coups (or coup attempts). Today’s Lula rally on São Paulo’s Avenida Paulista was the biggest political demonstration we have ever seen. pic.twitter.com/SkP0Nyw4y4 — BRASILWIRE (@BRASILWIRE) October 24, 2026 They held hands. People waved. Signs filled the crowd. People chanted. Tears fell. The crowd sang Lula’s chant over and over again: “Olê, olê, olê, olá, Lula, Lula.” “I will always stand with the president. It doesn’t matter that this is the final rally,” said teacher Gabriela Demétrio, speaking to a team reporting for Brasil de Fato, in the crowd. “I don’t believe in an ‘end.’ Lula is the greatest of them all,” The procession began near the corner of Rua Pamplona, ​​but upon reaching the São Paulo Museum of Art, moving forward became impossible. The “red sea of ​​people” that Lula was navigating made it impossible for the march to continue. Amidst the singing of Lula’s campaign jingles and the chanting of slogans, the crowd belted out the Brazilian national anthem, followed by cries of “long live democracy,” “never again to dictatorship,” and “long live Lula.” Standing in the middle of the crowd, Lula asked those present to let him step out of his car so he could climb onto the sound truck where the camera operators were positioned. “I want to see this sea of ​​people,” Lula said, asking for space to be cleared so he could safely exit the vehicle and reach the truck. Despite the immense crowd filling the street, he managed to get through; from the truck, he waved to the crowd, blew kisses, and held up both the flag of Pernambuco and another banner that read “the people, for the people.” The event concluded on a note of great joy. A sense of a mission accomplished, the result of a massive mobilization that shifted the course of the runoff campaign and may well leave an indelible mark on Brazilian history.

articles.title: Brazil: Lula Wins Stunning Upset Over Flávio Bolsonaro in Blow to Far Right & Trump
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : Well, I’m in Denver to speak after the screening of the film about Democracy Now! , Steal This Story, Please! , at CU Boulder this afternoon at 3:30. But right now we go to today’s top headline. We begin in Brazil, where President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has pulled off a stunning comeback to defeat far-right challenger Flávio Bolsonaro, but Bolsonaro is refusing to concede. Just three weeks ago, Bolsonaro won the first round of voting, but on Sunday, Lula defeated him by more than 4 million votes. Flávio Bolsonaro is the son of Brazil’s former far-right President Jair Bolsonaro, who remains under house arrest after being sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup following his defeat to Lula four years ago. Lula supporters celebrated in the streets of Brasília last night. STELA SAÍGUI: [translated] This turnaround was historic. I think we sent a message to the world that the fight against fascism is real, and it takes popular mobilization. Nothing surpasses the power and strength of the people. ANABEL FERREIRA : [translated] Oh my god! I can’t even believe it. It was a real struggle. We fought against some very powerful forces — economic power, betting companies, Meta, the media, the mainstream media, militia members and everything else — and we made it. AMY GOODMAN : On Sunday night, Brazilian President Lula addressed supporters in São Paulo after he was declared the winner in the runoff. PRESIDENT LUIZ INÁCIO LULA DA SILVA : [translated] But I wanted to thank the Brazilian people for the generosity they have shown me for a long time, and in the second round, to thank the generosity of the Brazilian youth who took to the streets, took to the streets to defend democracy. … I saw many scenes today of people being carried by their grandchildren to go vote, people unable to move around, people with cancer and other types of illness. And people went to vote because we were able to convince them that the vote was very important to safeguard democracy in the country. … I want to thank society as a whole, what really won. This election was an election in which we had to overcome outside interference through digital platforms, which we will have to regulate … in a demonstration that this country does not accept being anyone’s backyard. AMY GOODMAN : That was Brazilian President Lula speaking last night. His opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, has called for the election results to be annulled, citing a decision by a Brazilian Supreme Court judge to keep polling stations open for an additional two hours because of bad weather in some regions — both candidates had reportedly requested the extension. Flávio Bolsonaro’s refusal to concede comes four years after his father, Jair Bolsonaro, staged a coup after Lula defeated him in the 2022 election. This is part of what Flávio Bolsonaro said last night. SEN . FLÁVIO BOLSONARO : [translated] What happened today was not normal. It was downright unacceptable. A Supreme Court justice, for the first time in history, a former lawyer for Lula, with a simple stroke of the pen at the request of a former partner, changed the rules of the game in the middle of the match. At 5:01 p.m., Justice Zanin, who is not a member of the electoral court and has trampled on the specialized judicial system, decided to postpone the elections by two hours. This has never happened before in Brazil’s history. It has completely undermined equality among Brazilians from different cities and states. … It is impossible to understand the election results in context, given when these events took place. We will take legal action. I will request that these elections be annulled. AMY GOODMAN : Brazilian President Lula’s victory bucks a rightward shift in Latin America. Over the past 18 months, Honduras, Chile, Bolivia, Ecuador, Costa Rica, Peru and Colombia all elected right-wing leaders aligned with the Trump administration. In addition, Trump ordered the U.S. military to abduct the leftist president of Venezuela, Nicolás Maduro. We go now to Porto Alegre, Brazil, where we’re joined by Michael Fox, freelance journalist, former editor of NACLA . He’s the host of Under the Shadow podcast , a joint project of NACLA and the Real News Network. He’s also the co-founder of the independent news site Panamerican Dispatch . You’re there on the streets of Porto Alegre, Michael. Can you talk about the response? This is unprecedented for a candidate to win after losing in the [first round], which just took place three [weeks] ago. Talk about the significance of Lula’s victory by 4 million votes and Flávio Bolsonaro refusing to concede. MICHAEL FOX : Yeah, it’s just unprecedented, absolutely, Amy. I mean, it was just incredible to be on the streets last night, to be there seeing people voting. My wife votes near here in a town called São Leopoldo, and she said that there were people coming in from the hospital, that they — like, they literally left the hospital. They were in their hospital rooms, but they had to get there. They had to vote. This is something that we’ve just never seen before. The amount of organizing, the amount of marches and rallies, campaigning, pamphlets that we’ve seen the last three weeks has been something that I have never seen in my entire life, ever, covering elections for decades in so many different countries. It is — it is absolutely unprecedented. And that’s why people, when they went out to vote, and last night when they started to see the results coming in, they weren’t quite sure what they were going to see. This poll, the latest, the latest numbers, it said it was neck and neck. Like, they could not tell who was ahead. And the only thing that they said was going to make or break the difference was abstention. If Lulu was going to be able to get enough people out there to win the vote, then he would win; otherwise, it’d be Flávio. And he got way more than enough, double, right? Like, I think it was 10 million more votes. And also, just one other detail here, Amy, he won by double the percentage that he beat Jair Bolsonaro four years ago. It’s just shocking. And it is really important for Brazil and really important for the region. Now, the fact that Flávio Bolsonaro came out and said he’s not going to recognize the results, it’s almost as if you can’t expect anything else. We know that four years ago, his father didn’t respect the results. And in a lot of ways, this is really just a justification for him then to whip up a storm amidst his supporters. Already, the Supreme Electoral Court, the two — so, the Supreme Electoral Court in Brazil is made up of two, three judges from the country’s electoral court — from the country’s Supreme Court and other court bodies within Brazil. The two main judges that are on the Supreme Electoral Court were both appointed by his father, Jair Bolsonaro. So, these people, who many people saw them kind of trying to help the Flávio Bolsonaro campaign, and the president, Kássio Nunes, the president of the Supreme Electoral Court, has already said that he thinks that everything that went down in the elections was legitimate and fine. And like you mentioned already, many of the — the extension of the voting extension, Flávio Bolsonaro himself had requested it in five different states because of adverse rain, in fact, here in Porto Alegre, Santa Catarina, São Paulo and a bunch of other places. So, this is not something that is likely going to impact the results of this election, but he’s going to use this as justification to whip his people up and to attempt to create denialism and to undermine the vote, without a doubt. JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Michael, I wanted to ask you specifically about this whole issue of the turnout, because Flávio Bolsonaro actually got more votes in this election than his father did four years ago, but it was just the enormous increase in Lula’s vote, where he had gotten about 60 million votes when he defeated Jair Bolsonaro, this time he got 64 million votes. And so it was just the enormous increase in the turnout. How was that accomplished? And also, what was the impact of the debates, from what you could tell, that Lula had with Flávio Bolsonaro during this runoff period? MICHAEL FOX : So, this is so important, because I think this is one of those lessons that, everywhere, people need to learn from what Brazil has just done. It was organizing on the ground, grassroots, and it was every day. Like, one of the biggest things was, literally, the day after that first vote, people were just — you know, Lula supporters were just — they couldn’t believe what had just happened, right? He had just lost two points. He was supposed to be ahead in the polls. Now it looked like Flávio Bolsonaro was six points up. What are we going to do? And the very next night, you saw students hit the streets in Niterói. And it was these images of students saying, “Uh-uh, not going to happen.” And why students? It was because what happened with Jair Bolsonaro four years ago — or, six years ago, right? Under his term, 2019 through 2022, one of the major things he went out at the very beginning of his term is he tried to cut budgets across the board for federal universities. He slashed budgets, froze budgets. And students rose up, and they saw — some of the very first, the biggest marches against Jair Bolsonaro were the student marches. And so, the students were the ones who were really in the streets, front and center, helping to lead, helping to guide these marches. But it wasn’t just that. You saw people, like — and they were talking, “Look, you have to talk to your neighbors. You have to talk to your relatives. You have to go — you know, you have to travel, you know, to go back to your place of voting.” It was this massive vote-getting campaign, people asking, “Hey, do you need rides to get to the polls?” big marches, big rallies to show their support, and so much hope. This was another thing I think that was really important, that Lula, literally the night that he lost, he said, “Don’t worry. It’s all good. I like — I like sudden death. I like the second round. You know, Bolsonaristas, get ready, because, you know, I’m going to defeat you.” And he did. And people felt that kind of excitement. So, I think that was really important. The other thing was online. So, this is huge. First off, Bolsonaro, just like the far right in general around the world and in the United States, they know how to use the memes. They know how to use AI, Meta, Instagram. And, of course, Meta, in this case, was clearly also biased and doing favoritism for Jair Bolsonaro. But what we saw was Lula supporters, they had an organized campaign of trying to use memes, using AI to get around — they call it fora da bolha — you know, break through the bubble that they had, to try and get into other areas, to try and get to those independents, to the 33 million people in Brazil who didn’t vote. And they were just able to do this incredible campaign online. And they really, really — and, of course, online, here’s the problem, is the fact that Big Tech, we know, it is under the control of Big Tech. They control the algorithm. We don’t know what it is. And they’re playing favorites. That was clearly the case in this moment, except for the fact that Meta says that they didn’t interfere in the elections. But that’s what happened. But, definitely, Lula and his supporters organized and organized and organized, and it is a lesson for people elsewhere. In terms of the debates, the very first debate was just — it was just insane, right? Because it was an attack show. There were no rules. But I think that what people got out of it was just how aggressive Flávio Bolsonaro was, how many lies he was doing. But it was just this back-and-forth. Now, the second debate had all these specific rules. You couldn’t stand behind each other. You couldn’t just directly attack each other. You actually had to kind of respond. But then, when they did fact-checking afterwards, it showed that, you know, most of Lula’s answers were true, and most of Flávio Bolsonaro’s answers were false, and he was actually throwing out false information. So, it’s hard to tell exactly, like, the impact the debates had, but I think that, overall, Lula came out looking just a little bit better, because people said, you know, he is — he’s a statesman, right? He is a diplomat, and that’s what he represents. And this is, of course, the difference between the attacking of the far right and what we see kind of all elsewhere, their use of language and hate and discourse in order to undermine kind of the democratic debate. AMY GOODMAN : Michael, I wanted to go to the debate Friday night, the final debate. This is Lula speaking after Bolsonaro called him “nine fingers.” PRESIDENT LUIZ INÁCIO LULA DA SILVA : [translated] I am going to use my time, because he said something extremely stupid, and I am not going to let that go. He called me “nine fingers.” I want him to understand something. There is someone here in this audience who knows what the world of work is like. That person is me. There is someone here who lost a finger while working. I lost my finger while working. I had to work at night. I had no choice but to work. I will not allow him to call me that again. I will not allow it. CÉSAR TRALLI : [translated] Silence in the audience, please. PRESIDENT LUIZ INÁCIO LULA DA SILVA : [translated] He has never worked a day in his life. He doesn’t know what a work permit is. The first job he ever had was given to him by his father. He worked with his father and stayed in Brasília, and now he comes here and calls me names. He will have to apologize. He will have to apologize, because Brazilian workers are watching. Millions of workers have suffered because of employers who force people to work long hours. I was underage, and I worked at night, because I either worked or I didn’t eat. I will not accept some rich guy with a highly questionable political practice coming here and calling me “nine fingers.” AMY GOODMAN : That was President Lula responding to Bolsonaro calling him “nine fingers.” Michael Fox, if you can talk about the difference in the class base between Bolsonaro and Lula, and, actually, if you see comparisons to what’s happening in the United States now with President Trump? MICHAEL FOX : Well, there are obviously comparisons with the United States, and that’s something that I dug into a lot in Brazil on Fire , my podcast, back from 2022. And part of this is the fact that it is class-based, but it’s also race-based. Like, you know that in northeastern Brazil, it’s kind of the poorest region of the Brazil, and it’s the largest Afro-Brazilian region. This is the area that Lula came from, right? This is where he’s from. He understands this place. This is the region that’s always voted en masse for Lula — right? — and in high, high percentages. Why? Because his social programs, his poverty alleviation programs, his development projects have completely changed the map of northeastern Brazil. It’s been extremely important. The southern Brazil, in general, is white. It’s middle-class, descended from Europe, Italy, Germany and whatnot. And these people vote more in favor of Flávio Bolsonaro or the Bolsonaro family, right? This is an area that was actually back — and I did some reporting on this a while back. Like, Santa Catarina, the state where I actually live, they had the largest Nazi party outside of Germany during the 1930s. This is an area where there are still neo-Nazis. And so, this is extremely important to understand the role these connections that it plays within the support for Flávio Bolsonaro. And it absolutely is a response, kind of a pushback from the white lower class, middle class — the same thing we see within Trump’s — to kind of the poverty alleviation programs, to the social programs that Lula has been able to roll out over the last 20 years, just kind of in a similar way that we saw with Obama. And so, the reaction that we’ve seen for, first, the election of Jair Bolsonaro in 2018, and then the attempt for also Flávio Bolsonaro of the far right, this rise of the far right, is very, very similar in this sense. JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Michael, I wanted to ask you about the impact of this result in the rest of Latin America. Of course, we’ve heard much about the rightward turn in many Latin American governments. But the two largest countries in Latin America, Mexico and now Brazil, remain under the leadership of left-wing leaders. In fact, Claudia Sheinbaum was among the first to congratulate Lula on his victory last night. And Mexico and Brazil still represent half of the total population of Latin America. MICHAEL FOX : I saw an article yesterday or the day before that said this is the most important election, if not in Latin America, in the world, after the U.S. election. And it’s exactly for that. Lula and Brazil set a mark, in that they said, “No, we’re not going to go down that route.” And it is — it is an absolute game-changer for the region. In my podcast, Under the Shadow , I focus on U.S. intervention in Latin America, and I’ve spent this entire year looking at what Trump has been doing in the region, from, you know, his invasion of Venezuela, the turning the screws around Cuba and everyplace else, meddling in elections up and down. This is the one country that’s been able to stand up and say no. And this is one of the most important countries in the region, because it’s the largest GDP . Literally, the population, the size is the same as all the rest of the countries of South America combined. And Trump knows that. This is why this was a huge priority for him, getting this to flip and getting a good friend of his, like Flávio Bolsonaro, in here. Remember, Flávio Bolsonaro literally traveled to the United States six times this year. He met with Trump in May and convinced Trump to put two Brazilian gangs on the foreign terrorist organization list of the United States. That’s the same kind of the excuse that the United States uses to meddle in other countries, right? So, clearly, Flávio Bolsonaro was clearly aligned with Trump. He had already told Marco Rubio that he was more than willing to hand over his transition team to the State Department, which is just mind-boggling. But so, this, that’s why this is so important, because, literally, we now have someone like Lula, who is going to continue to stand up. Brazil is going to continue to stand up, demand sovereignty. Don’t forget that just last year we saw Trump levy 50% tariffs on Brazil, and then, you know, Brazilians rose up and said, “Uh-uh, that’s not going to happen,” and until, finally, like, you know, he had to — they negotiated, and then he removed them, because that’s not — you know, so this is an extremely important moment for the region. Brazil is a shining beacon for the region at this moment. And Brazilians know it, and so do so many people elsewhere. AMY GOODMAN : Michael Fox, we want to thank you so much for being with us, freelance journalist, former editor of NACLA , the host of Under the Shadow podcast , which is a joint project of NACLA and The Real News Network, co-founder of the independent news site Panamerican Dispatch , speaking to us from Porto Alegre, Brazil. To hear this interview in Spanish, you can go to democracynow.org . Coming up, we go to Serbia, where a student-led movement has pulled off an historic election victory, ending 14 years of the right-wing rule of Aleksandar Vučić. Stay with us. [break] AMY GOODMAN : Tom Morello performing “Flesh Shapes the Day” 10 years ago at Democracy Now! ’s 20th anniversary.

articles.title: Serbia’s Student-Led Movement Ousts Strongman Aleksander Vučić in Shock Election Result
articles.content: Serbia’s longtime leader Aleksander Vučić has been swept out of power by a historic student-led opposition movement against Vučić’s right-wing Serbian Progressive Party. Candidates from the Student List, who are not students themselves but largely first-time politicians selected by student-led popular assemblies, won a majority of seats in Sunday’s parliamentary elections, marking a seismic shift in Serbian politics. Their victory comes two years into a student-led movement sparked by the collapse of a roof at a train station in the city of Novi Sad, which killed 16 people. The disaster became a focal point for anti-government protests over corruption, cronyism, political violence and democratic backsliding. “Students really changed the whole political landscape of the country, and maybe even more important, they changed political imagination. They changed our understanding of what’s politically possible for all of us,” says journalist Lela Vujanić, who speaks to us from Belgrade about the groundbreaking elections. “This was a great democratic opening and democratic awakening, not only for the students, but for the rest of the country also.”

articles.title: Will Ousting Netanyahu Change Anything for Palestinians? Diana Buttu on Upcoming Israeli Elections
articles.content: Israeli parliamentary elections are being held on Tuesday, the first since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack and Israel’s subsequent assault on Gaza. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is currently embroiled in a corruption scandal in Israel, is up for reelection. On Friday, after two Israeli soldiers were killed at a checkpoint near Hebron, just days before Israeli polls are set to open, Netanyahu announced heavy restrictions on the movement of Palestinians out of the West Bank. Since then, Israeli forces have detained and expelled thousands of Palestinian residents from the area and begun home demolitions to clear the way for future Israeli settlements. “The reason that they’re doing this is because this entire election is about who is going to be tougher on Palestinians,” says Palestinian human rights lawyer Diana Buttu. “What [Netanyahu is] trying to do in the lead-up to this is say to Israelis that ’I’m the only person who can provide you with security.’ So, while lighting the place on fire, he’s also selling water.” Buttu explains that Netanyahu’s opponents across the Israeli political spectrum are equally punitive toward Palestinians. “The fact that you have all of these parties that are advocating major war crimes and nobody is blinking says something very deep about Israeli society, but also about an international community that has fostered this and that has allowed this to brew for all of these years.”

articles.title: Pink Floyd’s Roger Waters Backs Lula: ‘For Marielle Franco, Go and Vote’
articles.content: British musician and founder of the legendary progressive rock band Pink Floyd, Roger Waters, posted a video on his social media channels expressing his support for the candidacy of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Waters harshly criticized far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, highlighting his ties to U.S. President Donald Trump. “[Flávio] Bolsonaro, who is the son of an asshole, he’s an asshole himself; he comes from a long line of assholes. He is in cahoots with the United States of America, who want to steal everything you have in Brazil, not just the Amazon rainforest, but also any minerals or anything that you might have,” he said. The musician also mentioned that he had met Lula, describing him as “a man who has worked for you all his life, and you should let him go on working for you.” He further encouraged Brazilians to vote, calling for a “90%, 95%, or 100% turnout.” “If you have a grandmother who can’t get out of her chair to go to the polling station, carry her. Put her on a donkey, put her in a car, take her to the polling station, and vote, vote, vote! Only you can save Brazil from the machinations of the gangsters who pretend to be the government in the United States of America and their allies in Brazil, like the Bolsonaros,” he said in the video. Waters also brought up the case of Rio de Janeiro city council member Marielle Franco, who was murdered in 2018 by militia members Ronnie Lessa and Élcio de Queiroz. Other individuals linked to the assassination have ties to Flávio Bolsonaro. In 2023, Flávio Bolsonaro allocated a parliamentary amendment to a project led by Robson Calixto, a militia member convicted for his involvement in the death of the left-wing city councilwoman. “They killed my friend Marielle Franco,” Waters recalled. “They murdered her. Do you remember that? I remember—I will never forget. For the sake of Marielle Franco, go out and vote this Sunday. Vote for Lula.” The full text of Roger Waters’s post: You have an election on Sunday in Brazil. I love Brazil. I’ve done many, many… My name is Roger Waters, by the way. I’m a musician. I’ve done many, many gigs there in Brazil. I love your country. So the two candidates are Bolsonaro, who is the son of an arsehole. He’s an arsehole himself. He comes from a long line of arseholes. He is in cahoots with the United States of America, who want to steal everything that you have in Brazil that’s of any value. Not just the Amazon forest, but also any minerals or anything that you might have. They want to give it to the Trump family and to Jared Kushner and those other arseholes in the ruling elite. Or Lula da Silva. I’ve met Lula da Silva. I’ve looked into his eyes. This is an honest man. And he’s a man who has worked for you all his life and you should let him go on working for you. Sunday, the important thing is turnout. Turnout. It was only 78% in the first round. We need 90%, 95%, 100% turnout. If you have a grandmother who can’t get out of a chair to go to the polling station, carry her, put her on a donkey, put her in a car, take her to the polling station and vote, vote, vote. Only you can save Brazil from the machinations of the gangsters who pretend to be the government in the United States of America and their allies in Brazil, like the Bolsonaros. OK, please, please, please remember. They killed my friend Mariella Franco. They murdered her. Do you remember that? I do. I will never forget. For Mariella Franco, go and vote on Sunday. Vote for Lula.

articles.title: Hundreds Protest at Meta Headquarters in Brazil Against Far-Right Bias
articles.content: Manifestantes usaram faixas, cartazes e bonecos para denunciar a atuação da Meta nas eleições | Crédito: Igor Carvalho/Brasil de Fato Protesters targeted the multinational corporation Meta, on Monday, October 19, in Itaim Bibi, a neighborhood in São Paulo. Meta owns WhatsApp, Instagram, and Facebook. According to the organizers, roughly 500 people showed up to protest in front of Meta’s headquarters in São Paulo. Those in attendance criticized Meta’s biased interference ahead of the Brazilian elections. “We cannot claim to have fair elections when a company uses its economic, technical, and technological power to tip the scales in public opinion, which is exactly what is happening,” said Dani Silva, executive director of Ctrl+Z, one of the organizations behind the demonstration. Sociologist and professor at the Federal University of the ABC, Sérgio Amadeu, agrees that Meta’s bias has hurt the campaign of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. “Meta has acknowledged that there were technical issues, but these issues only harm one side: that of President Lula,” he said. “It is very difficult to imagine a Brazilian politician having a post with higher engagement than international artists like Beyoncé. Yet, that is what has been happening in Brazil with the [far-right Liberal Party congressman] Nikolas Ferreira. The Meta group is interfering in the election in a brutal way.” Camila Moraes is the secretary-general of Brazil’s National Union of Students and an activist with the youth group, Levante Popular da Juventude. She said that the country has to work to regulate social media platforms. “We cannot allow Donald Trump, Elon Musk, and Mark Zuckerberg to continue profiting from lies and manipulation,” Moraes said. “We must defend Brazilian sovereignty, and that is only possible under a Lula administration.” During the election race, the social media accounts of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva were negatively impacted. Meta acknowledged that “technical incidents” affected the ability to promote content posted by the candidate. In a statement, Meta addressed accusations that it had influenced the Brazilian election by favoring the candidacy of Flávio Bolsonaro. “Meta does not take sides in this or any other election, and allegations that we are favoring or interfering on behalf of any candidate or political group are false and unfounded,” Meta said. “Our systems do not rank or distribute content based on political ideology, and our rules, as well as their enforcement, apply equally to everyone.”
